title: Tools and Function Calling
why: In lecture 3 the model extracted a booking from text, but it couldn't tell us whether a table is free: it can't see our database, so it either makes things up or refuses. Today we give the model tools — our C# methods: the model asks for a call, our code runs it, and the answer is built on real data from our database. This is the foundation of every AI assistant and agent.
outcomes: You'll explain the function-calling loop: list of tools → call request → our code runs it → result → answer
You'll turn a C# method into a tool with `AIFunctionFactory.Create` and `[Description]` and pass it in `ChatOptions.Tools`
You'll run the loop automatically with `UseFunctionInvocation` and see in `response.Messages` which tool the model called
You'll write a good tool: a verb name, a description, typed parameters; and explain why today's tools only read

review.q: Does the model call our C# method itself? Describe the loop step by step.
review.a: No · 1) us: the question + the list of tools · 2) the model: a call request (name + arguments) · 3) our code runs the method and sends the result · 4) the model: a text answer · at least 2 requests to Gemini

review.q: The model can't see a tool's code. How does it learn what the tool does and when to call it?
review.a: From the name, the description (`[Description]`) and the parameters' JSON Schema · so a bad description = the tool is called at the wrong time or not at all

review.q: What does `.UseFunctionInvocation()` do? What would happen without it?
review.a: It runs the loop for us: sees the request, calls the method, sends the result, returns the final answer · without it `GetResponseAsync` would return a call request instead of text and we'd have to write the rest ourselves

review.q: Why `CheckAvailability(DateTime at, int guests)` and not `Check(string data)`?
review.a: The name says what it does · typed parameters go into the schema as exact types — the model doesn't have to guess a format and we don't have to parse a string · `[Description]` on each parameter

review.q: Why did we give the model only read tools today? What would be the problem with `create_booking`?
review.a: The model would call a writing tool by itself — it might take “8” as 8 a.m. and not ask the user · writing needs confirmation (human-in-the-loop, lecture 15)

quiz.explain: The model only returns the tool's name and arguments. Our code calls the method and sends the result to the model.

quiz.q: The model called `check_availability` and then wrote a text answer. How many requests went to Gemini?
quiz.explain: The first — the question and the list of tools (answer: a request). The second — the history and the tool's result (answer: text).

options: The model decided it doesn't need a tool — that's normal
quiz.explain: Whether to call a tool and which one is the model's decision.

quiz.q: “Four of us, tomorrow at 8” — why do we put today's date in the System prompt?
options: So the model can work out the `at` parameter from “tomorrow” — it doesn't know today's date
quiz.explain: The model is stateless and its knowledge stops at its training date (lectures 1, 3).

quiz.q: Why don't we give the model a `create_booking` tool today?
